item.title: To beat China on AI, Washington must first earn Americans' trust
item.description: Trump has positioned America to lead the AI race against China, but earning public trust through commonsense AI guardrails is the key to winning.
item.content:encoded:
America is in a race with China to lead the world in artificial intelligence (AI), and under President Donald Trump, America has every opportunity to win. AI will shape the global economy, strengthen our national security and determine which nations set the rules for the next generation of technology. We cannot afford to let China get ahead. But winning that race will require more than developing the world’s most advanced technology. It will require the confidence and trust of the American people.

The Chinese Communist Party understands what is at stake. Beijing is pouring resources into AI development, determined to dominate an industry that will shape global commerce, military capabilities and economic power for decades. New reports suggest China could lead the world in key areas of AI by 2030, while Chinese companies are already developing competitive technology at a fraction of the cost.

But America has a decisive advantage China cannot replicate: freedom. The Chinese Communist Party mandates adoption of its technology. In America, families, businesses, workers and consumers have the freedom to choose what works for them.

AMERICA CANNOT WIN THE GLOBAL AI RACE IF AMERICANS ARE AFRAID TO USE AI

That freedom is not a weakness; it is one of our greatest competitive advantages. It drives innovation, encourages competition and creates a technology ecosystem that is accountable to the people it serves. Protecting that advantage means earning public confidence in the technologies we develop.

Americans want to embrace innovation, but they also want confidence that it will work for them. Parents want to know their children are protected when interacting with AI chatbots. Seniors deserve protection from increasingly sophisticated scams. Workers want to know that AI will create opportunities, strengthen American businesses and make them more productive rather than leave them behind. These are legitimate concerns and Republicans should be leading the conversation with practical solutions.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS QUESTION WHETHER AI’S PROMISE OUTWEIGHS ITS RISKS

Recent polling makes clear that AI is becoming a major issue for American voters. Fifty-two percent of Americans are more concerned than excited about AI's growing role in daily life, and 79% expect AI to reduce American jobs over the next decade. A Navigator Research survey that the share of voters ranking AI among their top five priorities for Congress and the president jumped from 7% to 21% as a top priority for Congress and the president, the fastest growth of any issue tested this year.

Republicans should recognize this moment for what it is: an opportunity to lead. President Donald Trump has made American technological dominance and competition with China a national priority. His administration has established the Super Intelligence Force (SIF) to advance American leadership. We should build on that momentum rather than allow Democrats to define the debate through fear, pessimism and calls for government-heavy approaches that risk slowing down innovation.

TRUMP ANNOUNCES NEW 'AI FORCE,' VOWS TO PROTECT INDUSTRY AS AI CZAR ANNOUNCEMENT NEARS

There is a way forward to build trust with Americans that Republicans can charter to not only win this issue against Democrats, but to beat China on the global stage, too: clear and strong AI guardrails.

The distinctly America First path forward is clear: establish clear, targeted, commonsense guardrails that protect Americans without strangling the innovation that makes our country exceptional. We should protect our children, combat fraud, defend consumers and give American workers the confidence that the companies will share the benefits of this technological revolution.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The choice is not between unchecked AI development and burdensome government regulation. It is between an American model built on freedom, innovation, accountability and opportunity versus a Chinese model built on centralized control.

President Trump has put America in a position to lead. Now Congress should build on these efforts by establishing commonsense protections that can deliver both technological dominance and responsible innovation. When we get this right, we won’t just have won the AI race against China. We’ll have ensured that the future of AI is built on American values, creates American jobs, strengthens American security and puts the American people first.

item.title: I talked with Trump. Will his final years lead to an immigration deal?
item.description: Trump signals he's open to negotiating regularization for nonviolent immigrants, but warns Democrats that impeachment efforts could kill any deal.
item.content:encoded:
It is test time again for Democrats. They know how to campaign against President Donald Trump when he is not on the ballot for the presidency.

But does the Democratic Party actually want to accomplish something for immigrants who are in the country illegally? Many of their candidates swept in by the blue tsunami of two weeks ago, campaigned on helping the millions of immigrants who entered the country illegally during President Joe Biden’s term. But will they deliver that group … anything?

Because if the Democrats actually want to do that, Trump is ready to begin negotiations.

TRUMP OPENS DOOR TO IMMIGRATION DEAL, BUT REPUBLICANS HAVE ONE CONDITION

If the Democrats actually wanted to accomplish something for immigrants who are in the United States without the legal right to be here, the new speaker of the House and the new majority leader in the Senate could present Trump many different and acceptable pieces of legislation addressing some or all of those immigrants. If the proposals are reasonable, a genuine negotiation would follow between the president and the Democratic majorities over what they both wanted, and each could get most of what they want done.

If Democrats want a blanket amnesty, that won’t work. If they demand a "path to citizenship and voting," that would be a bridge too far. But if they seek "regularization" of people who are nonviolent and willing to work?

TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY

On Thursday, I asked Trump: "If Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer come up, and they want the DREAMers, or they want regularization for people who aren’t violent in the country, what are you going to want?"

The president didn’t respond directly to that hypothetical, but instead suggested there was room to negotiate on healthcare issues. "[G]reat things can be done between the Democrats and the Republicans on healthcare," Trump said. "And if I can do that with the Democrats, I’d love to do that."

DEMOCRATS PLOT MASSIVE SPENDING SPREE AFTER MIDTERM ROUT — AND TRUMP COULD HELP THEM PULL IT OFF

That exchange followed the president laying out a "condition precedent" of sorts (the legal term for an event or requirement that must occur or be satisfied before a contractual obligation becomes enforceable or a party is required to perform its side of any deal).

"So you can negotiate," I observed to the president. "But if they’re impeaching you, can you negotiate with the Democrats if they’re trying to destroy you at the same time?"

TRUMP SAYS HE 'CAN'T IMAGINE' DEMOCRATS WILL IMPEACH HIM A THIRD TIME

"Maybe not," the president replied. "Maybe I wouldn’t want to, because it’s in such bad, you know, when I negotiate, I negotiate in good faith. If they’re doing that, it’s in bad faith."

So, quite simply, every potential subject of legislation, including "regularization" of millions of illegal immigrants, is on the table when the new Congress arrives, but the table itself vanishes if the Democrats want to investigate rather than legislate.

THE MISTAKE NEWLY-ELECTED DEMS ADMIT THEY CAN'T AFFORD TO MAKE WITH TRUMP AFTER SWEEPING 2026 WINS

That’s a reasonable position from the president, but it is hard to see the incoming wave of democratic socialists, plus "the Squad" in the House agreeing to anything that could be termed a compromise, no matter the upside for the immigrant community.

To get to a deal, the "get Trump" Democrats would have to set aside their deep desire to grandstand so that they could accomplish some sort of security for the 10 to 20 million immigrants in the United States who are in danger of deportation if they cross the path of ICE.

AT LEAST 9 NEW DEM MEMBERS WILL CARRY AL GREEN'S MANTLE AND TRY TO IMPEACH PRESIDENT TRUMP

Which is why the immigrant communities have their hopes up. The goal of the conditional right to remain — a felony conviction would of course end a conditional visa — is within reach.

But such hopes were dashed by President Barack Obama when he had his large majorities in both the House and the Senate in January 2009, and again by Biden in January 2021 when he was supported by majorities in both houses of Congress. Both men abandoned this constituency.

JEFFRIES PROMISES ‘REMEDIAL ASSISTANCE’ TO ANYONE IMPACTED BY TRUMP IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT

Because being a Democratic leader means never having to say you are sorry to the people who trusted you.

Immigrants should not get their hopes up, as Democrats have a record of amnesia about them when they have legislative majorities.

Which is why the exile the GOP is about to enter in Congress isn’t remotely permanent or even likely to be long. Democrats have proven incapable in the past two decades of actually delivering anything for their coalition partners. Their big achievements? Obamacare under Obama and a flood of spending under Biden. The former wrecked healthcare delivery in the U.S., and the latter ignited the inflation which remains between 3% and 4%, that, while much lower now than its peak in the Biden years, is still the primary reason the GOP got the boot on Nov. 3.

Democrats have a short window in which to prove to the voters who are "up for grabs" —immigrants and their extended families, friends and communities — that it won’t be a "third strike."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

President Trump will want something in return for his signature, and that is most likely funding for the "Golden Dome," a U.S. missile defense system, and the Golden Fleet, which includes plans for nuclear-powered guided-missile warships.

Will the Democrats actually deliver? Doubtful, but perhaps their youngest elected members of the House and Senate will urge them to turn from the impossible-to-win battles for impeachment to the real stuff of legislative accomplishment.

item.title: Trump kicks off high-stakes Asia trip with Xi, Putin meetings looming on world stage
item.description: President Donald Trump is set to sign a trade deal with Thailand at the ASEAN summit before heading to China for historic talks with Xi Jinping.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump is in Asia for historic talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin this week, with nuclear arms reductions and Iran on the agenda and Trump signaling Monday that he also plans to raise Russia's war in Ukraine.

Trump's trip began Tuesday in the Philippines at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before he travels to Shenzhen, China, for Thursday's meeting with Xi and Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The rare gathering comes amid simmering U.S.-China trade tensions and ongoing conflicts involving Russia and Iran, with Trump signaling plans to raise denuclearization and efforts to end the fighting.

At the ASEAN summit, Trump is expected to sign a joint statement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul announcing progress toward a trade agreement. The president is also set to meet with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. before departing for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China.

TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA

The president has also raised the possibility of meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un during his visit to China this week, telling reporters Monday that talks could take place.

When reached for additional comment about the floated meeting, the White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump's remarks to reporters on Monday.

Trump is expected to discuss Iran and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during Thursday's highly-anticipated trilateral meeting, despite U.S. officials previously telling ABC News that Ukraine likely would not be on the agenda.

Trump notably told reporters on Nov. 8 that he plans to discuss denuclearization and ending the war in Iran during the trilateral meeting, DW News reported.

"We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran," the president said at the time.

Trump's trip also comes amid a scandal involving Nvidia, the American tech giant whose powerful AI chips are at the center of growing tensions between the U.S. and China.

Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned last week following reports of an affair with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of sharing information with Beijing, raising fresh concerns about Chinese espionage and access to sensitive American technology.

Trump cast doubt on the espionage allegations Monday, telling reporters he was unsure whether the woman was a Chinese spy. He also said he would be open to Huang returning as CEO.

TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING

The president will be joined by several high-profile figures during his Asia trip, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is accompanying Trump to the Philippines and China this week, according to Rubio's public schedule.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk is also expected to join Trump for part of his trip to China for the APEC summit, U.S. officials confirmed to CNBC on Friday.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chairman of the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, told CBS News’ "Face the Nation" in an interview on Sunday that he does not anticipate any agreements related to the reduction of nuclear weapons will be made this week.

"I don’t believe any agreements are going to be made, but certainly China has resisted being part of any agreements," Moolenaar told CBS News. "And if there’s a way to provide more security for the American people through those kinds of discussions, I think it’s important to have it."

Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

item.title: Buttigieg trashes Duffy’s ground stop response, but his DOT failures doom his 2028 bid
item.description: Pete Buttigieg's criticism of Sean Duffy's airline ground stop response is backfiring, reviving scrutiny of his supply chain absence and #WheresPete era.
item.content:encoded:
Seeking attention and perhaps absolution, presidential wannabe Pete Buttigieg threw himself into the controversy over last week’s airline ground stop; it did not go well. The former secretary of transportation desperately wants to be taken seriously as a 2028 candidate but is struggling to gain much of a following, currently ranking fifth in surveys of potential Democratic contenders. Maybe that’s because most people remember what a lousy job he did during the Biden years, a record he is foolishly inviting us to review. Source

Sensing an opportunity to make headlines and rewrite his history, Buttigieg was quick to criticize Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s press conference about the shutdown of our airports, saying, "You can just write down the comic book asterisk swearing characters." Source

BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS

And then Buttigieg held a press conference, claiming he was "like everyone else, very concerned about what's going on in the national airspace." He acknowledged he had no "inside knowledge" about what was happening and therefore had nothing to say. If Duffy’s presser was insufficient, Pete’s was pointless.

Pete goofed. By piling on his successor during the shutdown, Buttigieg is reminding us of his own shortcomings as transportation secretary, his only credential even remotely deserving of a promotion to the White House. Unfortunately for Pete, his Cabinet term is widely considered to have been a disaster, best known for his eight-week disappearance at the peak of a critical supply chain shortage brought on by COVID-19. With hundreds of ships lined up at the nation’s ports unable to unload cargo, and goods of all kinds running out as Christmas loomed, AWOL Buttigieg earned #WheresPete mockery on Twitter.

Turns out, the former South Bend mayor was home enjoying an extended family leave (he and his partner adopted twins who were born prematurely). Finally outed by Politico, Pete returned – not to work opening up the ports and solving other supply bottlenecks — but to a heavy schedule of media appearances. Unapologetic about his absence and devoid of solutions to the supply chain crunch, the secretary blamed consumers for an excess of demand, even as he pushed for more of Biden’s mammoth spending bills that fueled the shortages in the first place.

Among other snafus on Pete’s watch, there was indeed a nationwide ground stop, the first since the security-related shutdown following the terrorist attacks on 9/11. The 2023 halt to air travel lasted around 90 minutes and was caused by the failure of a system meant to alert pilots to hazards such as closed runways.

FAA GROUND STOP TIMELINE: WEEKEND CHAOS GROUNDS PLANES AND POSTPONES GAMES

That breakdown was one of many signals that our decrepit air traffic system needed repair – repair that Buttigieg neglected to provide. As Duffy posted on X: "Mayor Pete failed for four years to address the air traffic controller shortage and upgrade our outdated, World War II-era air traffic control system."

According to Duffy, DEI-obsessed Buttigieg bungled efforts to expand the number of air traffic controllers in part by lowering the acceptance requirements for training, leading to delays in the process and a surge in dropout rates at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City. In less than two years, Duffy turned around the program; as a result, the FAA announced last month that it exceeded its fiscal 2026 goal by hiring 2,235 air traffic controller trainees, the most in FAA history. Source Source

FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP

Buttigieg weakened the credentials needed to become an air traffic controller in a search for a more diverse pool of candidates. Like most of the Biden administration, he prioritized equity and diversity in the FAA trainee pool over building up the capabilities of the critical industry.

But it wasn’t only racial diversity he pursued. In 2024, Fox News reported that "the Federal Aviation Administration is actively recruiting workers who suffer ‘severe intellectual’ disabilities, psychiatric problems and other mental and physical conditions under a diversity and inclusion hiring initiative spelled out on the agency’s website." Source

Should Pete run for president, critics will question this initiative. They will also wonder why only $5 billion of the $25 billion allocated to the FAA under the bipartisan infrastructure law went toward upgrading air traffic control towers and systems.

EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP'S FAA TOUTS NEW AI-POWERED TOOL HELPING THOUSANDS OF PASSENGERS AVOID FLIGHT DELAYS

Voters may also question the sluggish pace of the administration's $7.5 billion electric vehicle charging initiative. While the 2021 infrastructure law aimed to catalyze a nationwide network of 500,000 public chargers by 2030 alongside private industry, bureaucratic hurdles and state-by-state permitting slowed the federal rollout to a crawl. Two and a half years after the bill passed, left-wing CBS’s Margaret Brennan pressed Buttigieg on "Face the Nation" over why only eight federally funded stations had actually come online—raising legitimate questions about whether federal red tape and domestic-sourcing mandates bogged down a signature transportation priority.

And then there was Pete’s special effort to "fix" our highway system, described by this NPR headline: "Pete Buttigieg launches $1B pilot to build racial equity in America's roads." The program, derided by Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis as the "woke-ification" of federal policy, was designed to "rectify harm caused by roadways that were built primarily through lower-income, Black communities after the 1950s creation of the interstate highway system." 

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Returning to the recent airspace closure, Pete tried to evade responsibility for our dilapidated FAA systems and rebuke Duffy, saying during a press availibity on Nov. 13 that was carried on C-SPAN, "We did a lot to upgrade the system. When we had an outage, I didn't stand there complaining about the Trump administration. We got to work... I'm certain that that's what career officials...at FAA and USDOT are doing. This should not be about politics."

But Pete didn’t get to work. In 2024, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported: "FAA determined that 51 of its 138 systems are unsustainable, citing outdated functionality, a lack of spare parts, and more. Over half of these unsustainable systems are especially concerning, but FAA has been slow to modernize. Some system modernization projects won't be complete for another 10-13 years. FAA also doesn't have plans to modernize other systems in need—3 of which are at least 30 years old." 

Buttigieg was too busy worrying about racist roads to fix our FAA, leaving Duffy a broken system, which he is attempting to modernize.

Yes, Pete, you’re right: It’s not about politics; it’s about performance. Too bad yours will keep you far, far away from the White House.

item.title: Trump arrives in Philippines ahead of Xi Jinping summit in China after GOP midterm losses
item.description: President Donald Trump arrives in the Philippines ahead of a historic summit with China's Xi Jinping, following bruising GOP losses in the US midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday as part of an Asia trip that will take him to China for a historic summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The trip marks Trump's first overseas visit since Republicans suffered bruising defeats in the US midterm elections.

Trump noted during a gaggle on Monday that while in China this week he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jingping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. 

"And then we go to China. And we'll be with President Xi, he was here a month ago. And we're also gonna meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un also," Trump said, referring to North Korea's leader. "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump later added.

Trump indicated that during the meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, they will discuss issues including denuclearization, Iran, Ukraine, economics and trade.

item.title: Duffy vows to modernize aging air traffic system after nationwide ground stop
item.description: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says Friday's FAA ground stop was no hack, as the FAA probes a router issue, network problem or installation error.
item.content:encoded:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Monday said he plans to modernize America’s aging air traffic control system and build new architecture that is "worthy of America" following a nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded more than a million passengers.

During an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity," Duffy said he wants to build a modern, resilient telecommunications network.

"Congress did give me $12.5 billion. That’s for radar and radios. I am well on my way to deploying all that money. You can’t buy this off the shelf, so I’ve ordered it. As it is delivered, we pay for it, and we deploy it into the NAS. But what’s really important is the next phase of the investment," he told host Sean Hannity on Monday.

The $12.5 billion in congressional funding is part of a broader effort to modernize the nation's air traffic control system, including communications, surveillance and other infrastructure.

DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

"So you saw a telecom issue on Friday. We’re replacing old copper wires with fiber, but this is an old architecture of a network. You’ve seen Newark go down. You’ve seen Dallas go down. You saw all of New York go down just a couple of months ago because of telecom issues. I want to build a brand-new architecture of a resilient telecom network that’s worthy of 2026 and worthy of America," he continued.

Duffy added that the department needs new software.

"The software we use to manage our airplanes in the airspace was built in the 1990s. It works. It works well. But if we’re going to drive more safety and more efficiency, we need brand-new software," he explained.

The secretary also said intelligence agencies found no evidence that a cyberattack forced the ground stop on Friday and that the Federal Aviation Administration was investigating whether a network problem, router issue or installation error caused the system failure.

The FAA is working with contractor L3Harris, which installed the router in question and is assisting with the investigation at its Florida laboratory.

"We had all of our intelligence agencies, at Donald Trump’s direction, talk on Friday night," Duffy said. "No one was seeing any kind of hack into our system. And we’ve now secured the router."

BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS

"We’re doing an analysis in Florida with L3Harris and the FAA. I actually asked the FBI to come in just to make sure, to put people at ease, that this was not a hack. So I think it was a network problem or a router problem or an installation error," he continued.

The roughly five-hour ground stop affected more than 1.5 million passengers whose flights were scheduled to depart on Friday afternoon and evening. More than 12,000 flights were canceled that day, according to the FAA, while delays and cancellations continued through the weekend.

item.title: Chargers, Justin Herbert finally win first game of season after brutal mistake by Ravens star
item.description: Justin Herbert and Omarion Hampton powered the Los Angeles Chargers past the Baltimore Ravens, ending their winless skid on "Monday Night Football."
item.content:encoded:
It’s happened, folks. There is no longer a winless team in the 2026 NFL season.

The Los Angeles Chargers have notched their first victory of the season, as Justin Herbert and company took down the Baltimore Ravens on "Monday Night Football," spoiling Jacoby Brissett’s first game with his new team since being traded by the Arizona Cardinals.

The Ravens’ troubles continue, as they dropped their fifth straight game and fell to 4-6 on a season that seems to be slipping away from them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Meanwhile, head coach Jim Harbaugh and everyone within the Chargers organization can all breathe a sigh of relief knowing they’ve at least avoided some embarrassing NFL history.

It was no easy feat against a desperate Baltimore team trying to right the ship in any way possible, especially at quarterback. The injuries to Lamar Jackson and Tyler "Snoop" Huntley have decimated the team’s offense, leading to a necessary trade with the Cardinals, who had made Brissett their third-string signal caller amid their own struggles.

The Ravens and its fan base hoped Brissett would be the answer to get the ball rolling again, but he was forced into a late fourth-quarter comeback scenario, down 23-20, but with ample time, and timeouts, to work with.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

On second-and-10 from their own 39-yard line, Brissett hit receiver Zay Flowers right between the numbers, and he crossed midfield into Chargers territory. But, instead of trying to get out of bounds or simply taking the first down and heading back to the huddle, Flowers tried fighting through two Chargers defenders.

It was a grave mistake.

Tarheeb Still made a tremendous play, stripping Flowers of the ball and Elijah Molden fell on it for a clutch fumble recovery with 2:11 to play in the game.

All Herbert needed to do was kill the clock with a couple of first downs, and considering he was doing everything in his power to will his team to victory on Monday night, he knew he was just about at the finish line.

Los Angeles did their jobs, with Herbert finding Charlie Kolar for a first down just after the two-minute warning. It was enough to melt the clock down to 18 seconds, and with no timeouts on their end, the Ravens couldn’t muster the miracle Hail Mary to avoid disaster as the pass from Brissett was batted down near the goal line as the clock struck zero.

In the end, the Ravens are not going to win games if Derrick Henry is rushing for only 10 total yards on 10 carries. He had nine rushing yards on 16 carries back in 2023 during his time with the Tennessee Titans, but this performance, or lack thereof, was astonishing to see, especially for a Ravens home game and considering the circumstances heading into Monday night.

No team rushing for a team total of 16 yards can function as an offense, and that’s credit to a hungry Chargers defense that certainly did their part in keeping Brissett uncomfortable in his first start for Baltimore.

Brissett did, however, look better once settled in the second half. He finished 33-of-49 for 340 yards, though he was unable to notch his first touchdown pass while throwing an interception. He seems to like tight end Mark Andrews, who had a team-high eight catches and 82 yards.

Meanwhile, Herbert was 12-of-18 for 129 yards through the air, but it was his legs that played such a vital role in the Chargers getting things done on the road. He was a running threat, rushing for 51 yards on seven carries with the game’s first touchdown under his belt.

Then, Omarion Hampton had the running performance he’s been searching for since the start of the season, racking up 105 yards on 22 carries with his own touchdown run.

While Harbaugh and his Chargers can celebrate and look to build off their first win, head coach Jesse Minter and his staff are back to the drawing board as their playoff hopes hang in the balance after handing their opponent its first win of the year.

item.title: DHS chief tells Americans to 'breathe' amid tech outages, insists homeland is 'secure'
item.description: Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says the homeland is secure after Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines and Microsoft experienced outages.
item.content:encoded:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin had a direct message for concerned Americans after the U.S. experienced a slew of technology disruptions that halted flights, email services and online banking platforms across the country.

"Well, breathe. The homeland is secure. Our banking system is secure and when something like this happens, we’re able to react and react fast," he said Monday on "Hannity."

Mullin’s remarks came as customers Monday reported trouble accessing online services of major U.S. banking platforms, including Wells Fargo, Chase, U.S. Bank and Bank of America. United Airlines also faced a widespread system outage on Monday that briefly affected departing flights.

UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’

The latest disruptions follow a nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday, which caused widespread flight delays and cancellations, as well as a separate Microsoft outage last week that affected Outlook email services.

Mullin maintained that the incidents were not a result of cyberattacks and described the disruptions as "individually unrelated."

DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

"I can tell you with 98% certainty we’re not seeing the cyberattack," the DHS secretary said.

"We’re not seeing the footprints going in. We’re not seeing the footprints going out," he continued. "And so, nothing points to it being connected."

FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Four banks reportedly faced outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com.

JPMorgan Chase said the problems were not related to cybersecurity issues in a statement to FOX Business, adding that customers still have access to their accounts and funds and that the company was working to fix the issue.

Mullin suggested the broader technology disruptions highlight vulnerabilities in aging infrastructure as newer technologies place demands on legacy systems.

"We just have a lot of technology thrown at us and our world runs on technology now," Mullin told host Sean Hannity. "We used to have backup systems and the backup systems are overwhelmed by the new systems now."

TRUMP INTEL CHIEF WARNS AI FIRMS ON HACKS, SAYS NEW DEPARTMENT IS THE 'COP ON THE BEAT'

Mullin also said a prominent technology expert briefed him earlier Monday and suggested to him that "super intelligence" could have contributed to the disruptions. The DHS secretary believed the theory "kind of makes sense."

"He said, because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is. And so when they put in a program that’s able to write codes, and it goes in and it self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself, it’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing. That’s a ripple effect," he explained.

"It causes these systems to be overrun that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today," he added.

Mullin defended the Trump administration’s response to recent technology disruptions and pledged to deploy federal resources to help companies experiencing technology problems.

"We are very secure, and I feel very comfortable about where we’re at," he said.

item.title: American basketball player’s Nigeria trip ends in arrest after officials spot him abandoning suspicious bags
item.description: Nigerian officials say an American basketball player abandoned two checked bags containing 75 pounds of cannabis before officers arrested him in a parking lot.
item.content:encoded:
A U.S. basketball player was arrested at a Nigerian airport last Wednesday after allegedly attempting to smuggle a large quantity of cannabis into the country in his luggage.

Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, a native of Savannah, Georgia, was linked to two checked bags containing 75 pounds of cannabis at Murtala Muhammed International Airport, according to Nigerian officials. Khiree reportedly arrived in Lagos aboard an Emirates flight from Thailand via Dubai.

While at the airport, Khiree appeared to abandon two checked bags containing a potent strain of cannabis known as "loud," according to Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA).

CBP OFFICERS SEIZE NEARLY 850 POUNDS OF KHAT PACKED INTO 12 SUITCASES AFTER FLIGHT FROM LONDON

"The suspect, who was placed under discreet surveillance upon arrival, was observed abandoning his two checked-in bags before attempting to exit the airport with only his carry-on luggage," officials said.

He was subsequently apprehended in the airport's parking lot, according to the NDLEA.

FEDS SEIZE $6.4M WORTH OF COCAINE ABOARD OIL TANKER AT PORT OF LOS ANGELES, ARREST SUSPECTED CARTEL SMUGGLER

Although Khiree claimed he was visiting Nigeria to build connections for his basketball career, a forensic examination of his phone reportedly uncovered evidence of drug trafficking.

"The suspect, a native of Savannah, Georgia, USA, who claimed he has lived in Thailand since October 2025 where he plays professional basketball, said he came to Nigeria on holiday to build networks for his basketball career," officials said.

"A forensic examination of his mobile phone revealed information pointing to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity."

Investigators also found that both bags bore Khiree's name tag and contained tracking devices. Authorities confirmed that the cannabis originated in Thailand.

item.title: Ro Khanna pitches $1,700 checks for Americans to offset Iran war costs: 'A chance to deliver'
item.description: Rep. Ro Khanna proposed a $1,700 refund check for every American family to cover higher gas, food and electricity bills tied to the war in Iran.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., on Monday proposed giving every American family a $1,700 refund check to offset higher costs driven by the war in Iran.

Khanna, a frequent critic of President Donald Trump's war in the Middle East, said the checks would be sent to every American family to reimburse them for the higher gas, food and electricity prices sparked by the conflict and resulting disruptions to oil transport routes.

The congressman said Democrats "have a chance to deliver" following their sweeping midterm victories earlier this month, urging the House and Senate to approve the payments in January.

"I want to give every American family a $1,700 check to make them whole for the war in Iran," Khanna said in a video posted to X.

RO KHANNA REJECTS WARNINGS THAT TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATIONS COULD DERAIL DEMOCRATS' AFFORDABILITY AGENDA

"This is to cover their higher gas prices, their higher food prices, their higher electricity bills. Now Democrats have a chance to deliver. The first week in January, the House and Senate must pass a $1,700 refund check to Americans. Let’s put it on Donald Trump’s desk," he continued.

Khanna had previously urged Congress to block all funding for the war.

Khanna also introduced legislation in September that would redirect certain unused Pentagon funds to compensate taxpayers and dependents for the economic costs of the war. The bill does not specify a $1,700 payment and has not advanced beyond the committee referral stage.

Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, estimated last month that the conflict in Iran had cost the average American household about $2,000, adding up to $265 billion nationwide. His estimate included higher energy costs, borrowing costs and military expenditures.

VOTERS HAVE A BLUNT MESSAGE FOR TRUMP ABOUT HIS IDEA TO DOLE OUT $5,000 CHECKS

Gas prices soared after the war began in February, with the national average rising above $4 per gallon before declining in recent weeks. The average was $3.81 per gallon as of Monday, about 75 cents more than a year ago, according to AAA. Diesel averaged nearly $6 per gallon, about $2.23 more than a year earlier.

Trump has repeatedly argued that higher prices are worth it to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon, although the president, Vice President JD Vance and other Republican leaders have acknowledged that the party's midterm losses were at least partially due to Americans' frustrations about higher prices.

Before the midterms, the president promised a $5,000 "Trump dividend" check to every adult U.S. citizen if the Republican Party retained control of the House and Senate, but Republicans lost control of both chambers.

TRUMP’S $5K CHECKS COULD JOIN STACK OF PAST UNFULFILLED PROMISES, FORMER CONGRESS BUDGET CHIEF WARNS

Several GOP leaders expressed skepticism about Trump's plan, pointing to concerns over the escalating national debt, potential inflationary pressures and the need for congressional approval.

It remains unclear if Khanna's proposal will receive the same pushback from Democrats.

Trump has previously floated or endorsed other similar payments in his second term that never materialized, including a $5,000 "DOGE dividend" tied to government savings and a $2,000 payment funded by tariff revenue.

item.title: Biden library nears site decision as fundraising trails ambitions: report
item.description: Joe Biden’s presidential library foundation is reportedly nearing a Delaware site decision after securing multimillion-dollar donations in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Former President Joe Biden’s presidential library foundation is reportedly closing in on a location in Delaware, even as its fundraising efforts continue to fall short of expectations. 

Despite receiving several multimillion-dollar gifts in 2026, the Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation is working to overcome a difficult fundraising start, following a roughly $600,000 deficit in 2025, according to filings reported by CBS News.

The foundation reportedly raised $1.5 million in 2025 but spent $2.1 million. An official told the outlet that the organization was not actively soliciting donations that year, characterizing it instead as a "building and infrastructure year."

The expenses, which were partly covered by contributions from Biden’s presidential inaugural committee and individual donors, primarily went toward staff, consultants and legal fees. Roughly $250,000 was specifically paid to consultants tasked with laying the groundwork for the foundation’s fundraising operation, the outlet said.

EX-DEM FUNDRAISER TORCHES BIDEN AS BOOK LAUNCH IMPLODES: 'NO ONE WANTS TO READ'

This year, the foundation secured two $5 million gifts among its donations, according to reports.

CBS News noted that the foundation is now seeking to capitalize on the post-midterm political climate, as wealthy Democrats reportedly poured money into campaigns that helped fuel sweeping victories for the party.

Despite this year's fundraising recoveries, some of Biden’s close allies have reportedly criticized Democratic donors for failing to proactively offer support for his library.

Biden has "never been a good fundraiser, even when he was in the Senate," one source said.

His wife Jill is also expected to help with fundraising as Biden undergoes treatment for prostate cancer.

JOE BIDEN SAYS CANCER SLOWED HIM DOWN, LIMITING MEMOIR PROMOTION TOUR

The foundation has also expanded its board with five new members, bringing in a mix of diplomatic, business and nonprofit experience as it seeks to strengthen its fundraising efforts, according to reports.

The reported additions include Elizabeth Frawley Bagley, Biden’s former ambassador to Brazil; Bijan Sabet, a venture capitalist and former ambassador to the Czech Republic; event planner Bryan Rafanelli; Wilmington nonprofit leader Logan Herring; and Annie Tomasini, a former White House deputy chief of staff.

OBAMA CENTER ISN'T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT'S AN ACTIVISM CENTER.

The library’s fundraising performance could offer a window into Biden’s standing within the Democratic Party and the extent to which wealthy donors are still willing to contribute to preserving his political legacy. His support among some donors has been strained by frustrations with his presidency and his decision to pardon his son, Hunter.

As Biden works to build financial support for the project, the foundation’s fundraising total still pales in comparison with that of President Donald Trump’s presidential library foundation, which has already secured tens of millions of dollars.

Trump’s donor list has been led in part by major media and technology companies that have aligned themselves with the president, including Meta, Elon Musk’s X and Paramount, according to reports.

item.title: Former USMNT coach says 'American sports reward losers' as he leaves for Manchester United
item.description: Mauricio Pochettino says American sports reward losers, blasting Major League Soccer's lack of promotion and relegation as he departs the USMNT.
item.content:encoded:
Americans are used to dominating just about every sport we care about, which makes our ongoing mediocrity in men’s soccer tough to swallow.

As former USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino heads to Manchester United after 26 months in charge, his takeaways from running U.S. soccer are a bad look for the program.

Coming from European football, trying to build a winner inside a system that cushions failure was a problem from day one. He summed up America's dilemma with soccer to Spanish newspaper El País during the 2026 World Cup.

"American sports reward losers," he said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Over in Europe, losing gets your club relegated and puts jobs on the line.

In Major League Soccer, nobody gets booted out of the league, and finishing in the cellar just gets you rewarded with a top draft pick. That setup completely kills the survival instinct you need to win at the highest level.

MAURICIO POCHETTINO TOLD USMNT PLAYERS 'WE'RE AMERICAN, WE DON'T TAKE S***' AHEAD OF WORLD CUP

"If you start in MLS and you haven’t won a game in three months and you’re at the bottom, what’s the consequence if there’s no promotion or relegation, no international competition? Pochettino said. "Soccer is different: if you reward those who don’t win, if you don’t have goals, you don’t fight. If I lose, what happens? Nothing. They just fire the coach."

Hard to argue with the guy.

American sports fans have been calling this out for years: U.S. soccer is overly corporate and flat-out soft when real trophies are on the line.

LA GALAXY COACH GREG VANNEY SAYS TEAM USA WAS 'TOO NAIVE,' EXPLAINS CHRISTIAN PULISIC'S STRUGGLES

"Also, the American player is disciplined, but with a sense of complacency that isn’t good in soccer," he said. "It took us a year and a half to change that mentality."

Nowhere was that battle against complacency more obvious than how Pochettino handled Christian Pulisic.

LANDON DONOVAN JOINS CHRISTIAN PULISIC CRITICISM FOLLOWING USA'S WORLD CUP EXIT WITH HARSH OBSERVATION

After Pulisic decided to sit out the 2025 CONCACAF Gold Cup, where the U.S. watched Mexico win the title in the final, Pochettino refused to give his most talented player the captain’s armband. He rolled with veteran Tim Ream at the 2026 World Cup, then passed over Pulisic again in October in favor of Tyler Adams. Pulisic can take over a game when he’s locked in, but putting up zero goals at a World Cup after taking a voluntary summer off raises fair questions about whether America’s biggest star has the grit to actually lead.

Even while keeping things friendly with the American soccer press corps, he clearly got tired of coverage that graded the team on a soft curve instead of holding players to real international standards.

"I understand the culture of football," Pochettino insisted.

To be fair, Pochettino’s point only goes so far. America’s closed-league setup keeps franchises financially stable instead of letting clubs go bankrupt like they do in Europe, and the USMNT’s 4-1 Round of 16 loss to Belgium showed that a tougher attitude won’t close a talent gap overnight.

TEAM USA ISSUES STATEMENT IN ENGLISH AND SPANISH AFTER DISASTROUS WORLD CUP EXIT

As U.S. Soccer starts looking at potential successors like Steve Cherundolo, B.J. Callaghan, Pellegrino Matarazzo and former Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola, whom Pochettino recommended for the job.

Until U.S. soccer stops protecting players from failure, this program is going to stay an afterthought when the real heavyweights show up.

item.title: Curt Cignetti fires back at Indiana 'easy' schedule critics: 'I really don't give a s---'
item.description: Indiana coach Curt Cignetti slammed critics of the Hoosiers' soft schedule, saying the narrative fuels the 9-1 team's chip with CFP rankings looming.
item.content:encoded:
Indiana Hoosiers head football coach Curt Cignetti doesn’t want to hear a peep about their strength of schedule compared to other College Football Playoff hopefuls.

Cignetti, whose team is 9-1 and 6-1 in Big Ten play, has remained at No. 6 in the AP Top 25 poll for the past five weeks, and is sitting at No. 9 in the CFP rankings.

The CFP committee will unveil another week of rankings on Tuesday, but the eight teams above Indiana all picked up wins like they did on Saturday, so there might not be much movement.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Either way, Cignetti was asked by a student reporter, Ian Plaskoff, on Monday during his news conference about his team’s conference record, and furthermore, how those teams have fared after facing them. In total, Indiana’s conference opponents are a combined 8-16, and Plaskoff believed it was indicative of how physical the Hoosiers can be rather than what the discourse has been about their schedule.

It is believed by some that Indiana has benefited from a weaker schedule not just this season, but in years past. In the last three years since Cignetti took over the program, they are 36-3.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Cignetti had time today to bash all those with that thinking.

"Well, you know, we don’t play anybody. We have a soft schedule, right?" he said. "That’s all I’ve heard around here for three years. People like to discredit us and what we’ve accomplished. … The good thing about it is, I think it feeds into our motivation and our chip. And that’s why I’m not afraid to keep it alive. And you know what? I’m 65 years old and I really don’t give a s---."

Cignetti acknowledged that his comments were going to only fuel the fire surrounding the Hoosiers’ "easy" schedule, but he didn’t care.

He went on to point out how Northwestern and Nebraska were both undefeated before playing them earlier this season. Their only blemish on the record was against Ohio State, who lost Julian Sayin during the game and hasn’t seen him return since.

Cignetti called it a "layup" that they missed in terms of losing to the Buckeyes, but their conference rival losing back-to-back games after beating them is being viewed as Indiana not facing a quality opponent in Ohio State.

"We ripped the heart out of that team," Cignetti said. "They haven’t been the same since without the quarterback. … We missed a layup."

Cignetti admitted, "You get tired of the narrative sometimes," but these are the reigning national champions. Yes, they are without their Heisman-winning quarterback, Fernando Mendoza, and many other key pieces of that undefeated squad from a season ago.

But convincing wins against Washington this upcoming weekend, and Purdue during "Rivalry Week" to close out the regular season, could turn the dial down on the outside noise.

item.title: Hillary Clinton picks a foreign politician she believes is now the ‘leader of the free world’
item.description: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton argued Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney may be the current "leader of the free world" instead of President Donald Trump.
item.content:encoded:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton argued during an interview aired Sunday that if any politician qualifies as the current "leader of the free world," it would be Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

MS NOW host Rachel Maddow interviewed Clinton at the Temple Emanu-El Streicker Center in New York City and asked, "Do you think that there is a leader of the free world right now?"

"Maybe Mark Carney," Clinton said.

"That’s what I was going to ask," Maddow said. "He’s certainly articulating a vision of the free countries of the world and of — of the liberty-loving nations of the world that is about being stronger together."

CARNEY CASTS HIMSELF AS NATO DEFENDER AMID TRUMP BEEF, DESPITE CANADA MISSING KEY BENCHMARK FOR DECADES

The relationship between the United States and Canada has been strained following President Donald Trump's suggestions that Canada become the 51st U.S. state and his decision to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

Clinton also argued that while some individual European leaders stood out, the continent as a whole was too disorganized. 

"And, you know, there are some good individual European leaders, but Europe has got to get itself organized so that, you know, the sum of the parts adds up to some kind of a whole and be able to do a better job at making some tough decisions, particularly with respect to Ukraine," she said. "They need to release the $250 million of Russian assets that are frozen in those Belgian banks and use it to defend Ukraine, just for starters."

"So if they can begin to make some collective decisions, then I think you’ll see other leaders emerge," Clinton continued. "But there’s going to be, as you know, Rachel, some very consequential elections in Europe this year, like the presidency of France. And if a populist pro-Putin party emerges with a leader who is very close to Putin and very beholden to Putin, Marine Le Pen, becomes the president of France, then we have new problems that we’re going to have to deal with."

TRUMP’S PROPOSED RUSSIA DEAL RAISES NATO ALARM AS EX-COMMANDER WARNS PUTIN SEEKS INFLUENCE OVER EUROPE

Earlier in the interview, Clinton argued that Trump had done "immeasurable damage" to America’s standing on the world stage with foreign policy that she described as "dangerous and incoherent.’

She also accused Trump of catering to "strongmen leaders."

"We are, unfortunately, seeing someone who admires strongmen leaders, thinks he is one, and believes in the old-fashioned concept of spheres of power," Clinton said. "And honestly, I don’t think it’s exaggerating to say that he’s perfectly fine with Putin doing whatever he wants with Ukraine and the rest of Europe." 

"He’s perfectly fine with Xi doing whatever he wants with Asia, as long as he can dominate the Western Hemisphere, and that all of them are some kind of triumvirate that is going to decide what the rest of us are capable of doing and what kind of society we will live under," she added. 

White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital, "President Trump is creating good-paying jobs, securing trillions of dollars in investments, and positioning our country to dominate the remainder of the 21st century. Meanwhile, Crooked Hillary Clinton is still whining about her spectacular 2016 election defeat. It’s time for Hillary to move on."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Morgan Murphy, a former White House official and former Pentagon press secretary, told Fox News Digital in response to Clinton's comments, "Canada's economy is chasing Mississippi's, and its armed forces couldn't scare the Salvation Army. It’s obvious Hillary still can’t admit the obvious: she lost [to] Trump, and he’s still the leader of the free world."

Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under Trump, also criticized Clinton's comments.

"Canada’s PM Carney is nothing close to being the leader of the free world," Wold told Fox News Digital. "The Canadian economy is contracting; Canadian culture is at its weakest point as a consequence of mass immigration and proliferating crime and budget problems; separatist movements across the Canadian federation are gaining strength; and most of all, to the extent Canada projects power at all, it does so only from within the sphere of U.S. power projection and military might in the Western Hemisphere, making Canada at best a younger sibling piggybacking on America’s power projection around the world."

"Carney, pretending to be 2026’s Marshall Tito, used several high-profile speeches to criticize the America First movement and pitch a small state ‘non-aligned movement,’" he added. "There are no takers for this idiotic gambit outside of EU cultural elites in the dying capitals of Europe."

FRONTIER PASSENGERS TACKLE MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY CHOKED OFF-DUTY FLIGHT ATTENDANT, TRIED TO OPEN DOOR MID-FLIGHT

item.title: Ecuador's president denies US operates military base despite reports of troop buildup
item.description: Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denies the U.S. operates a military base at Taura Air Base, describing American personnel's activities as temporary.
item.content:encoded:
Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denied that the United States operates a military base in his country after an Agence France-Presse (AFP) investigation signaled an expanded U.S. military presence at an air base near the port city of Guayaquil.

"Sometimes there's a specific mission. Sometimes there's a specific operation," Noboa told the news outlet Altavoz, describing U.S. personnel at Taura Air Base as carrying out "temporary activities" under a bilateral security agreement, including intelligence-gathering drone flights.

"We work together. It's not an American base. It's an Ecuadoran base," he commented.

THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN

Noboa's remarks came about a month after AFP had documented an unusual deployment of U.S. military aircraft, dozens of tents and construction of new infrastructure at the air base.

The investigation identified approximately 20 U.S. military flights arriving at Taura between June and mid-October, along with internal documents confirming the presence of American troops.

Several flights originated from U.S. military installations, including Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point in North Carolina and Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, with stopovers in Puerto Rico and Panama.

The buildup also raised legal concerns among senior Ecuadorian military officials.

AFP cited a September letter in which then-Air Force commander Gen. Mauricio Salazar asked military leaders to clarify the legality of the deployment. Salazar was subsequently removed from his post and reassigned to a less senior role, the report said.

The increased U.S. military presence comes after Ecuadorian voters rejected a Noboa-backed referendum in November 2025 that would have amended the country's constitution to lift its ban on foreign military bases.

US MILITARY BOARDS, SEARCHES AND SINKS VESSEL ALLEGEDLY SUPPORTING LOS CHONEROS NARCO-TERRORISTS

Despite the referendum's defeat, Quito and Washington have deepened security cooperation to combat drug trafficking and transnational organized crime.

Human Rights Watch has described the United States as Ecuador's primary security partner in its crackdown on organized crime, providing equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support.

The watchdog characterized the partnership as "perilous," warning that "both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fuelled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war."

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, President Donald Trump has designated several Latin American cartels as foreign terrorist organizations and authorized military strikes against vessels in international waters suspected of drug trafficking.

WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES

Ecuador has also emerged as a key ally in Trump's crackdown on drug cartels and narcoterrorism, with U.S. and Ecuadorian forces working together to intercept narcotics shipments and dismantle transnational criminal networks, the country's foreign minister told Fox News Digital in September.

 Roberto Kury said closer cooperation with Washington had delivered "a lot of positive results" in recent months, citing drug shipments intercepted through U.S. intelligence and joint operations.

"There is an intelligence (sic) and cooperation from the United States, but there is also always the presence of Ecuadorian military or police. They work together," Kury told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

"Most of the drugs go to the United States. So that’s why the United States shares the problem," Kury said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also praised Ecuador as the United States' most "aggressive" partner in its Western Hemisphere crackdown.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Southcom for comment.

item.title: Trump admin opens civil rights probes into 15 colleges over DEI grants
item.description: The Education Department's Office for Civil Rights opened probes into CUNY's NYC Men Teach program over alleged race- and sex-based discrimination.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Department of Education announced Monday that it has opened federal civil rights investigations into several teacher preparation programs following complaints alleging race and sex-based discrimination.

According to a department press release, the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) formally opened the probes on Friday, Nov. 13, targeting programs "designed to recruit, retain, and support future educators" that allegedly "provide sex or race-specific recruitment, support, and financial opportunities for candidates in violation of civil rights laws."

The initial four entities under investigation are the City University of New York (CUNY), the University of Maryland College of Education, the Minnesota Department of Education, and the Minnesota Office of Higher Education. The department noted that OCR is also opening investigations into 11 additional universities over similar allegations.

DEPT OF ED PUSHES AHEAD WITH EFFORTS TO DISMANTLE FEDERAL BUREAUCRACY AFTER BLUE WAVE

The department said OCR will examine whether the programs violate Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin, or Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, which prohibits sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programs.

Specifically, federal investigators are examining:

* City University of New York (CUNY): Under investigation over its NYC Men Teach program for alleged discrimination on the basis of both race and sex.

* University of Maryland: Under investigation for alleged racial discrimination in its administration of the Maryland Higher Education Commission Teacher Quality and Diversity Grant Program and the EdTerps CARES Network.

* Minnesota Department of Education: Under investigation for alleged racial discrimination through its Education Tuition Assistance Program, which provides scholarships and stipends to students in teacher preparation programs.

* Minnesota Office of Higher Education: Under investigation for alleged racial discrimination in its administration of the Minnesota Aspiring Teachers of Color Scholarship Pilot Program and the Underrepresented Student Teacher Grant.

A NEW YORK UNIVERSITY FACES JUSTICE DEPARTMENT INVESTIGATION OVER 'BLACK MALE INITIATIVE'

A spokesperson from the Minnesota Office of Higher Education told Fox News Digital: "The Minnesota Underrepresented Student Teacher Grant (USTG) was established by the Minnesota Legislature in 2021. OHE is implementing this program in accordance with State law," 

"The Minnesota Aspiring Teachers of Color Scholarship was a pilot program also established by the Minnesota Legislature in 2021. This scholarship is no longer available to Minnesotans as funding ended after the 2024-25 academic year," the spokesperson added.

The investigations stem from complaints filed by the Equal Protection Project (EPP), a legal advocacy group founded by Cornell Law School professor William Jacobson as part of the Legal Insurrection Foundation.

"The Equal Protection Project welcomes the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights' decision to open investigations into complaints alleging violations of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964," Jacobson told Fox News Digital, adding that his organization will cooperate fully with the investigations. 

"The opening of these investigations reflects OCR's determination that the allegations warrant further review and underscores the importance of ensuring that all students have access to educational environments free from discrimination based on race, color, or national origin," Jacobson added.

MINNESOTA YANKS RACE-BASED GRANT AFTER DOJ INITIATED CIVIL RIGHTS REVIEW, DOJ REVEALS

EPP chief counsel Maureen S. Riordan echoed that sentiment, calling the decision "an important step toward addressing serious concerns regarding compliance with federal civil rights protections and ensuring that educational institutions uphold their obligations under Title VI."

A Department of Education spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "The Department will open investigations across the nation based on credible reports that universities with education programs withhold opportunities for recruitment and financial support from candidates based solely on race," adding, "Teachers are the heartbeat of our schools, and the Trump Administration will ensure a future where students are [judged] based on their merit and grit, not the color of their skin."

The enforcement push aligns with President Donald Trump’s effort to eliminate diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives since he returned to office in January 2025. Shortly after his inauguration, Trump signed executive orders aimed at ending DEI programs across the federal workforce and federal contracting, directing agencies to enforce civil rights laws in alignment with the Supreme Court’s 2023 Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard ruling, which struck down race-based affirmative action in college admissions.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS

Department officials previously told Fox News Digital that the administration, led by Education Secretary Linda McMahon, plans to intensify efforts to dismantle federal bureaucracy, strengthen parental rights, and enforce federal civil rights laws against higher education institutions following Democratic victories in key midterm elections earlier this month.

A CUNY spokesperson told Fox News Digital: "CUNY is proud of its role educating the teachers of tomorrow and our programs are open to all students regardless of race, gender or national origin." 

The University of Maryland declined to comment. The Minnesota Department of Education did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Netflix's 'Untold' series tackles the New York Giants' miracle Super Bowl XLII upset of the Patriots next
item.description: Netflix's "Untold: One Giant Upset" lands Dec. 21, featuring Eli Manning, Michael Strahan, and Tom Brady on the Giants' shocking Super Bowl XLII win.
item.content:encoded:
Christmas came early for Giants fans. It's not Jaxson Dart's return, though all of New Jersey is eagerly waiting for that day.

Netflix announced on Monday that a new installment in the Untold series will drop Dec. 21. Titled One Giant Upset, the documentary focuses on the miracle New York Giants team that upset the Patriots in 2008.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Netflix's Untold has previously unpacked the wildest sagas in sports, from Manti Te'o's catfishing scandal and the Malice at the Palace brawl to Johnny Manziel and Urban Meyer's Florida Gators. Now, Big Blue gets the spotlight.

ELI MANNING FINALLY REVEALS WHY HE WRIGGLED HIS WAY OUT OF PLAYING FOR CHARGERS

Are they going to retell stories we've all heard in the nearly two decades since the G-Men won that ring? Of course. Will it be sweet to revisit the night Eli Manning and company broke New England's team of destiny? Absolutely.

For Giants fans, that 2007 squad remains unforgettable because of how ugly things started. New York opened 0-2 with head coach Tom Coughlin on the hot seat before rattling off 11 straight road wins, including playoff upsets in Tampa, Dallas, and minus-one-degree Green Bay.

SUPER BOWL CHAMPION PLAXICO BURRESS COMPARES PLAYING FOR JETS TO HIS TIME IN PRISON: 'A F—KING LOSER'

After trading haymakers with New England in a 38-35 Week 17 loss, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo unleashed his four-end NASCAR pass rush in the rematch: Super Bowl XLII. Michael Strahan, Justin Tuck, and Osi Umenyiora sacked Tom Brady five times, holding the historic offense to 14 points.

Then came the legendary fourth quarter: Manning slipping out of three jerseys, David Tyree pinning the football to his helmet, and Plaxico Burress — playing on a torn ankle ligament — hauling in the winning score.

TOM BRADY ADMITS TO MORE MOTIVATION AFTER DEFLATEGATE SUSPENSION, REVEALS WHAT HE DID WHILE AWAY FROM PATRIOTS

Manning and Strahan lead the documentary's Giants lineup alongside Coughlin, Spagnuolo, Tuck, Shaun O'Hara, Antonio Pierce, Sam Madison, Burress, and Tyree, joined by Brady.

Hearing Brady get honest about the toughest loss of his career adds real juice to the show. Still, watching Netflix celebrate one of the landmark games in NFL history highlights a total joke.

DREW BREES GIVES HIS STANCE ON ELI MANNING'S PRO FOOTBALL HALL OF FAME CANDIDACY AMID STRONG DEBATE

Super Bowl XLII defined an era, and Manning owns two Super Bowl MVPs against the Belichick-Brady dynasty, yet the Pro Football Hall of Fame has passed him over twice. Make it make sense. Leaving the architect of football's biggest upset out of Canton is a Giant mistake.

item.title: Democratic judge under fire for releasing violent offenders calls bail law a ‘direct assault’ on rights
item.description: Judge David Carpenter called Alabama’s Aniah’s Law a ‘direct assault’ on constitutional rights, citing defendants’ presumption of innocence.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic Alabama judge facing mounting scrutiny over past decisions to release violent offenders is criticizing a state law that allows defendants charged with certain violent crimes to be denied bail.

Circuit Court Judge David Carpenter called Alabama’s Aniah’s Law a direct assault on constitutional rights, arguing that defendants should not be held indefinitely based solely on criminal charges, citing the constitutional presumption of innocence.

In a social media post, Carpenter argued that critics of government overreach involving license plate cameras, such as Flock cameras, are not equally concerned about expanded pretrial detention laws.

"Can someone explain to me why the people who are so alarmed that a flock camera might spot their car on a public road, and they call that government overreach, are silent on the fact that voters across the country keep overwhelmingly passing new laws to empower the government to hold you in jail indefinitely on the basis of a charge only," Carpenter said.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

"These laws, like Alabama’s Aniah’s Law, are a direct assault on the Constitutional guarantee of the presumption of innocence. But no one is talking about this at all, much less expressing the hysteria associated with having a camera see a license plate," he said.

Although Aniah’s Law was originally passed in 2022, Alabama voters approved a major constitutional amendment this year expanding the law to cover additional offenses. The expansion added attempted murder, solicitation or conspiracy to commit murder, and discharging a firearm or explosives into an occupied dwelling, building or vehicle.

"We are all one accusation away from being a criminal defendant," Carpenter said in a post on Facebook.

WHITE HOUSE CALLS DC POLICIES 'INSANITY' AFTER 19-YEAR-OLD GUNMAN GETS PROBATION IN SHOOTING

Carpenter has faced controversy over several judicial decisions over the years. Local outlet 1819 News reported that he previously described himself online as a "far left, liberal, progressive, democratic socialist."

In April 2023, Carpenter approved a plea deal for Damien McDaniel, who was arrested in 2019 for shooting two people in a car when he was 17 years old, 1819 News reported. After being released from jail, McDaniel allegedly went on a 14-month shooting spree across Alabama, killing 18 people and injuring more than 30 others.

Carpenter also granted bond to Raukeem Cunningham in connection with the 2022 shooting death of a teenage girl, the outlet reported. While out on bond, Cunningham was arrested and charged with fatally shooting three people at a Bessemer gas station in 2024, prompting the revocation of his original bond.

In addition, Carpenter reportedly dismissed a 2015 rape charge against Fredrick Terrenda Hampton in 2019, according to reports. The dismissal came just two days before Hampton met Paighton Houston, who later disappeared. Her body was found buried behind a home after she died of an accidental overdose.

CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE

Hampton pleaded guilty to abuse of a corpse in connection with Houston’s death, and Carpenter gave him a 20-year split sentence with only three years to serve in custody, the outlet said.

Houston’s mother ultimately asked Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall to investigate Carpenter over his decision to release Hampton, whom critics described as a repeat sex offender.

During his campaign for judicial office, Carpenter said one of his major goals was to "reform the criminal justice system in Alabama."

"If elected, I will work to reduce the number of repeat offenders while addressing the expensive problem of prison overcrowding in Alabama," he said.

item.title: James Comer launches bid for Kentucky governor
item.description: House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., is launching a campaign for Kentucky governor Monday night, a source familiar with the plan says.
item.content:encoded:
House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., is launching a campaign for governor on Monday night.

"Serving this state is a calling for me," Comer said during a tele-townhall. "Kentucky needs a leader whose policies will lead to growth and good-paying jobs. We need a leader whose priority will be to reduce taxes so Kentuckians can keep more of what they earn."

Comer teased a "major announcement" for Monday night earlier in the day. A source familiar with his plans told Fox News Digital it would be his long-awaited campaign to lead the commonwealth of Kentucky.

REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES

Comer spent the majority of his announcement fielding questions from Kentuckians on topics like education, small business, and high prices.

Among the policies he advocated for was reducing Kentucky's income tax to zero.

"We all talk about attracting new businesses and new industry to Kentucky," Comer said. "If we can get that existing income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state and help our state grow into the future."

Kentucky's gubernatorial election will take place in November 2027, with the primaries set for May of that year.

Gov. Andy Beshear, who is widely considered a potential contender for the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, is term-limited.

Comer ran for Kentucky governor in 2015 but narrowly lost the GOP primary to former Gov. Matt Bevin.

But this election cycle will likely see the House lawmaker enter as the frontrunner for his party's nomination.

Comer has served in the House of Representatives since November 2016, when he won a special election for Kentucky's 1st congressional district. Since then, his profile has skyrocketed as the top Republican on the House Oversight Committee for the better part of the last six years.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE

As committee chairman since Republicans took back the House majority in 2023, he's launched investigations into former President Joe Biden's use of autopen and the federal government's handling of Jeffrey Epstein's case, among others.

And despite Beshear's popularity as the state's two-term Democratic governor, Kentucky has historically been seen as a red state.

President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris by roughly 30 points there in 2024. He beat former President Joe Biden there by 25.9% in 2020.

item.title: Illegal alien accused of attempted murder at large after Rikers release despite ICE detainer: DHS
item.description: Delon Raymond Jaundoo, a Guyanese citizen in the United States illegally, was freed from Rikers Island despite an ICE detainer, according to DHS.
item.content:encoded:
A Guyanese citizen living in the United States illegally remains at large after being released from custody in New York City earlier this month, despite facing multiple violent felony charges and an active federal immigration detainer, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

DHS officials stated that Delon Raymond Jaundoo was arrested in Brooklyn on charges including attempted murder, first- and second-degree assault, criminal use of a firearm, and multiple counts of criminal possession of a loaded weapon.

His prior criminal record also includes an arrest for third-degree assault.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged an immigration detainer for Jaundoo on April 29, which the New York City Department of Correction declined to honor, allowing him to be released from Rikers Island.

MANHUNT UNDERWAY FOR VIOLENT ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO WAS RELEASED UNDER NYC SANCTUARY POLICIES

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticized New York’s sanctuary policies following the release, arguing that state and local laws prevent cooperation with federal immigration authorities even in cases involving violent offenses.

Jaundoo lawfully entered the country during the Obama administration but overstayed his authorized stay, which expired in January 2015, according to DHS.

"Despite these violent charges, sanctuary politicians in New York refused to honor ICE’s detainer and released this criminal back onto the streets to put more American lives in danger," Mullin said in a statement. "Under Governor Kathy Hochul, New York has become a hotbed of illegal alien crime."

DHS SECRETARY BASHES NEW YORK LEADERSHIP AFTER ANNOUNCING THOUSANDS OF ARRESTS IN SWEEPING OPERATION

"The sooner we put an end to these reckless sanctuary policies, the sooner we can all work together to make America safe again," he added.

Jaundoo's release comes amid ongoing restrictions on local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

HOCHUL BOASTS 'I JUST BANNED IT' AS NEW YORK OUTLAWS LOCAL POLICE PARTNERSHIPS WITH ICE

Upon taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed an executive order limiting city coordination with ICE, and a state law signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul took effect in August barring local authorities from cooperating with federal immigration officials.

DHS stated that several other illegal immigrants arrested for or convicted of violent crimes, including murder, arson, assault, and rape, have similarly been released from custody under the state's current policies.

"Governor Hochul has been clear: New York State is not and never will be a sanctuary for violent criminals," a spokesperson for Hochul told Fox News Digital. "By law, New York State always notifies federal immigration enforcement of any non-citizen serving a State prison sentence. Any assertion otherwise is a blatant mischaracterization of the facts meant to distract from the cruelty and violence we’ve seen from Secretary Mullin’s ICE agents."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Mamdani's office for comment.
